children.blurb: Testing arguments before peer review covers the work a researcher does to stress-test a paper's claims, reasoning, evidence, and framing before submitting it to a journal or conference.

children.blurb: Disciplinary register and language in academic writing and peer review covers how fields such as machine learning, cognitive science, linguistics, and medicine use distinct vocabulary, sentence patterns, citation habits, and levels of formality.

sections.body: AI in academic writing and peer review is now used for drafting sections, checking arguments, adjusting disciplinary register, screening for plagiarism and AI-generated text, and explaining published work to wider audiences. Authors use language models to outline manuscripts, propose transitions, and rewrite passages for clarity, while editors and reviewers use similar tools to check consistency and flag suspicious text. The work is not fully automated, because peer review depends on judgment about novelty, methods, and significance that current systems do not reliably supply. AI can summarize literature and suggest missing citations, but it can also invent references, misread results, and reproduce biases in the training data. In practice, these tools sit alongside human authors, reviewers, and editors rather than replacing them.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Some parts of this field are settled enough for routine use, such as grammar checking, reference formatting, and basic plagiarism screening against large corpora. Other parts remain contested, especially AI detection, which produces false positives and false negatives and can disadvantage writers who use English as an additional language. Testing arguments before peer review is only partly solved, because a model can surface counterexamples or missing steps but cannot certify that a claim is correct or that a study will survive review. Drafting assistance is useful for standard sections, yet it struggles with original theoretical contributions and with the tacit conventions of a discipline. The honest limits include fabricated citations, shallow synthesis, confidentiality risks when text is uploaded to third-party services, and the difficulty of attributing responsibility when AI contributes to a manuscript. Peer review itself is not solved by AI, and no current system can replace expert evaluation of methods, ethics, or significance.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader can begin with Drafting a Manuscript for the practical work of turning notes and results into a submission-ready text. Testing Arguments Before Peer Review then shows how to stress-test claims, look for gaps, and anticipate reviewer objections before a paper goes out. Disciplinary Register and Language explains how conventions differ across fields and how AI can help or harm a writer's voice and precision. Plagiarism and AI Detection covers originality checks, the limits of detection tools, and the integrity questions that arise when generated text enters the process. Explaining Research After Publication turns to summaries, translations, and other ways to reach readers once the paper is out, and the site's library holds 135 research papers that can serve as examples of the finished form. Together these pages move from first draft to post-publication reach, with each one addressing a different point where AI touches academic writing and peer review.
